question: What is the main difference between skin traction and skeletal traction?

options.A: Skin traction requires surgical pins placed in the bone
options.B: Skeletal traction uses much lighter weights than skin traction
options.C: Skin traction uses external devices attached to the skin
options.D: Skeletal traction is only used on the upper extremities

explanation: Skin traction applies pulling force from the outside using tapes, boots, or straps, while skeletal traction uses pins or wires placed directly into the bone. You've got this!

question: Why can't we use heavy weights in skin traction?

options.A: Too much weight causes bones to fuse together too quickly
options.B: Heavier weights will snap the traction rope instantly
options.C: Heavy weights interfere with the hospital overhead pulley system
options.D: Higher weights cause skin breakdown and tissue injury

explanation: Since the pull relies on soft tissues, too much weight will tear or blister the skin instead of helping the bone. Great job learning the basics!

question: Why do we use skin traction right after a bone fracture?

options.A: To speed up the growth of new skin cells
options.B: To completely eliminate the need for pain medication
options.C: To permanently heal the bone without surgery
options.D: To relieve painful and violent muscle spasms

explanation: Steady pulling tires out the muscles around the break, stopping those painful spasms that pull the bone ends out of place. Keep up the good work!

question: A patient with a broken hip is placed in skin traction mainly for which reason?

options.A: Preventing deep vein thrombosis in the affected leg
options.B: Immediate rehabilitation and walking exercise practice
options.C: Permanent alignment so surgical repair is no longer required
options.D: Temporary stabilization and comfort while waiting for surgery

explanation: Think of skin traction here as a helpful temporary pause—it keeps the leg steady and comfortable until the surgical team is ready. You're doing great!

question: What is the most common type of skin traction used for lower limb injuries?
explanation: Buck's extension is our go-to straight-pull skin traction for temporary leg injuries on the ward. You'll see this a lot in clinicals!

question: Which infant condition is Bryant's traction typically used to treat?
explanation: Bryant's traction gently lifts both of a baby's legs straight up in the air to help realign a dislocated hip. Nursing pediatrics made simple!

question: What must you always check regarding traction weights during patient care?

options.A: Ensure they hang freely without touching the floor
options.B: Remove them every hour to let the muscles rest
options.C: Increase the weight if the patient complains of pain
options.D: Rest them on a stool when turning the patient

explanation: Weights must hang completely free! If they touch the floor or bed, the pulling force stops working. Simple check, big impact.

question: What happens if a traction rope slips out of its pulley groove?

options.A: The patient's blood pressure will drop rapidly
options.B: The pulling force on the extremity is lost
options.C: The fracture will heal twice as fast

explanation: If the rope rubs against the bed frame instead of the pulley, the mechanical pull stops and the traction won't work. Good thing you're checking your equipment!

question: Which sign tells you there might be nerve compression in a limb with skin traction?

options.A: Rapid healing of the skin surface
options.B: Dark brown discoloration of the nails
options.D: Numbness and tingling in the toes

explanation: Numbness and tingling (paresthesia) are classic warning signs that pressure is building up on the nerves. Always listen when patients report these feelings!

question: How often should you check the circulation and nerves (neurovascular status) of a limb in skin traction?

options.A: Only once a day during the morning shift
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain

explanation: Checking frequently helps you catch circulation or nerve issues early before any permanent damage happens. You are learning to be a vigilant nurse!

question: What is a common complication directly caused by skin traction straps and boots?

options.B: Total loss of joint flexibility forever
options.C: Skin breakdown and pressure ulcer formation
options.D: Severe infection inside the bone marrow

explanation: Constant pressure from boots and tapes can easily irritate the skin. That's why regular skin checks are a nurse's best friend!

question: A patient in Buck's extension says their heel feels like it is burning under the foam boot. What is your best immediate action?

options.A: Inspect the skin under the boot for redness or pressure damage
options.B: Permanently cut off the traction straps without telling anyone
options.C: Add an extra weight to the rope to lift the heel higher
options.D: Administer a strong sleeping pill to help ignore the sensation

explanation: A burning feeling is an early warning sign of a pressure sore. Taking a quick look underneath can prevent a major wound!

question: What device can a patient in lower limb skin traction use to safely lift their body for position changes?
explanation: The trapeze bar lets patients use their upper body strength to lift their hips for bedpans or back care without messing up their traction alignment. Brilliant setup!

question: Why is emotional and psychological support so important for patients in skin traction?

options.A: Mental fatigue prevents the patient from eating hospital meals
options.B: Anxious patients have higher rates of bone infection than calm ones
options.C: Psychological stress stops the traction weights from pulling correctly
options.D: Bed confinement and restricted movement cause significant anxiety and frustration

explanation: Being stuck flat in one position is tough on the mind as well as the body. A kind word and clear communication go a long way in nursing care!
